paras.x: I was being delivered like livestock. That was the first thought that came to me as the wooden caravan groaned up the mountain road.
The second thought was that livestock were probably treated better.

I sat alone in the back of an old gypsy caravan as its wheels rattled violently over roots and stone. Every bump sent my body crashing against wooden walls lined with hanging charms, faded fabrics, old perfumes, and discarded trinkets from journeys long past. The entire carriage smelled like flowers left too long in a graveyard.
An old elven driver sat outside steering the black stag that pulled the wagon. He had spoken exactly two words to me since dawn.
That was eight hours ago. Since then, silence. Just me. Just this road. And the increasingly horrifying destination waiting ahead.

I am Alfar Chandralon. Second son of House Chandralon of the Arayan Empire. The unwanted middle child. My older brother would inherit our estates. My younger brother remained protected because mother adored him. And me? I was apparently "the son who needed hardship." The son who needed discipline. The son who needed to "become useful."

That was how father phrased it while volunteering me to become ward and squire to Captain Hannah Icetear. As if he were gifting me some grand opportunity. As if he were not quietly sacrificing me to satisfy a peace treaty. I clenched my jaw.
Six months ago, the war between elves and humans had finally ended. Or so the politicians called it. Ended. Such a gentle word for what happened to "Snowwinter". Now called "Ashwinter".

One of the grandest elven cities ever built had burned beneath human fire bombardment. White towers collapsed. Ancient libraries turned to smoke. Entire bloodlines vanished overnight. And leading that attack? My uncle. High General Cassian Chandralon. The butcher of Ashwinter. The man many humans praised as a hero. The man every elf wanted dead.
And now his nephew was being sent directly into the heart of the most dangerous elven military faction alive. Wonderful. Truly magnificent planning by my family.

The road became steeper. Rougher. The clean forest we passed earlier slowly transformed into something darker. Branches twisted overhead like skeletal fingers. The sunlight weakened. Birdsong disappeared. Even the wind seemed afraid to enter this place.
I leaned toward the carriage opening. Then I froze.
Movement. High above. At first I thought they were shadows. Then I saw long war bows. Red cloaks. Steel blades. Women.
Tall elven women perched high within the trees like predators. Watching us. Dozens of them. Silent. Still. Beautiful. Terrifying.
"Do not look at them too long."
He let out what might have been amusement.

Wonderful. Even the driver had decided honesty was appropriate now that death felt closer. The caravan rolled forward another fifteen minutes. Then I saw it. And forgot how to breathe. The Verdant Gate.

It rose from the forest like a kingdom hidden inside a living fortress. Massive wooden walls stretched endlessly across the forest boundaries. Watchtowers climbed into the sky. Thick wooden spikes faced outward. Massive crimson banners bearing silver-white tree insignias hung from the walls. Vines crawled across ancient timber. Guard platforms overflowed with armed female elves. Archers lined elevated walkways. Mounted rangers moved along the roads below. And carved into the massive central gate:
Beyond it? Towns hidden inside forest walls. Not a camp. Not a fortress. A militarized civilization. The old driver stopped.
I stepped into cold mud, with my backpack. The moment my boots touched ground, conversation stopped. Every nearby ranger stared at me. And dear gods. I was not dreaming. I'm here, the Crimson Veil.

They were even more intimidating up close. Tall. Nearly all of them towered over me. Six feet. Some taller. Athletic bodies carved from years of warfare. Leather armor. Steel plating. Crimson cloaks. Scarred skin. Perfect elven faces. Predatory eyes. Beautiful enough to belong in palace paintings. Dangerous enough to cut those paintings apart.
One spat near my feet. Another openly laughed. A third looked disgusted.
I adjusted my coat and attempted dignity. "I am Alfar Chandralon, second son of House Chandralon."

Terrible decision. The entire gate erupted in laughter. Even the old driver sighed. One red-haired ranger stepped forward. She was absurdly tall. Her crimson cloak moved behind her like spilled blood. Twin daggers rested at her hips. Her green eyes studied me like I was an insect. Then she smiled. It was not kind.
The laughter died. Everything changed. The atmosphere became colder. More dangerous. Another ranger muttered.
My stomach dropped. I raised both hands.
"I had nothing to do with that." I yelped.
The red-haired ranger walked closer. Her face now inches from mine.
Silence. Wonderful. Now I was shouting at murder elves. My survival instincts continued to impress. Her eyes narrowed. Then..

Her fist slammed into my jaw. The world exploded. Mud hit my face. Pain screamed through my skull. I tasted blood immediately. The surrounding rangers laughed. One poured ale onto my back. Another kicked dirt onto me. Humiliation burned hotter than pain.
The red-haired ranger grabbed my hair and yanked me upward effortlessly. Her strength was absurd.

The gates opened, and I entered hell. Inside was a sprawling military city built into nature itself. Massive barracks, Training grounds, Blacksmiths, Weapon racks, Mounted units, Tower bridges, Tree platform sniper nests, Underground tunnels, Watch posts, Market lanes, Medical halls, Execution platforms.

Everywhere I looked: Women. Beautiful. Powerful. Armed. Watching me. Judging me. Hating me. And somewhere deeper inside all of it. Captain Hannah Icetear waited. The woman my family had gifted me to. The woman who would decide whether my future involved training…Or suffering.
As I walked deeper into the city of crimson warriors, one horrifying realization settled into my bones. If the women at the gate were merely guards…What kind of monster commanded them?
And why did I suddenly feel like my life had already ended the moment I crossed Verdant Gate?

The ranger leads me up a wooden stairway slick with rain and moss. My jaw still aches from where I was struck at the gate. My coat smells like mud. Ale. Blood. And humiliation. A wonderful perfume for noble introductions.
The towering red-haired ranger walking ahead of me says nothing as we climb. She moves with terrifying balance despite the rain-slick platforms. I nearly slip twice trying to keep up.

Below us, the Red Rangers settlement stretches endlessly. What I once believed was a war camp reveals itself to be something far worse. An empire of killers. Wooden towers rose through ancient trees. Rope bridges connected elevated watch posts. Training fields below were filled with screaming warriors.

I watched two female elves spar with curved blades while another group practiced archery from moving platforms suspended high above the forest floor. Blacksmith fires roared. War drums echoed. Mounted rangers galloped through muddy roads. And everywhere…those crimson cloaks. Hundreds of them. The ranger glances back at me.
I quickly lower my eyes. She smirks.
We continue upward. Eventually we reach the highest section of the fortress. A massive wooden hall built directly into the trunk of an ancient tree. Its doors alone are twice my height.
Two heavily armored guards stand outside. Unlike the women below, these guards do not laugh. They do not sneer. They simply stare at me as if calculating how quickly they could dismember me.

One opens the door. Warm air hits me first. Then silence. The inside of the chamber is vast. Dark polished wood. Massive maps pinned to walls. War banners hanging from high beams. Ancient elven weapons mounted like sacred relics. The faint smell of steel, parchment, and cedar smoke filled the room. And at the center, she sat waiting.

Captain Hannah Icetear. For a moment, I forgot every intelligent thought I had ever possessed. She was beautiful. In the same way lightning is beautiful before it kills someone. Golden hair flowed over crimson and silver-white armor. Sharp elven features carved with impossible precision. Cold green eyes. Perfect posture.

She sat behind an enormous carved desk like a queen pretending not to wear a crown. Two elite rangers stood beside her. One hooded. One red-haired. Neither moved. Neither blinked. I suddenly understood why everyone outside feared this room.
Hannah rested her chin against her knuckles as she studied me. No emotion. No rage. No hatred. Which somehow felt worse.
Her voice was soft. Elegant. Controlled.
The ranger beside me shoved me forward. I collapsed onto my knees. My palms slammed into polished wood flooring. Pain shot through my bruised jaw. I looked up.

Silence. She slowly rose from her chair. And gods...she was taller than I expected. She descended the steps from her platform with terrifying calm. No rushing. No anger. Just certainty. Her boots echoed through the chamber. She stopped directly in front of me. Then grabbed my chin. Forced my face upward. Her grip was iron.
That hurt far more than the punch. The two guards behind her laughed softly.
Hannah released my face. I fell forward onto my hands.
"Do you know why you are here?"
"To serve as your squire?" i answer uncertainly.
"You are here because your empire owes us blood."
Silence swallowed the room. My heartbeat pounded violently.
Interesting. So the rumors were true. She despised her own queen. Hannah studied me carefully.
Then she smiled. It was somehow colder than rage.
The hope died immediately. The hooded guard chuckled.
"You will clean weapons. Wash armor. Serve food. Train. Bleed. "And if I find even a fragment of your uncle inside you…"
"I will personally hang your bones above Verdant Gate."
She smiled again. A beautiful monster.
Every instinct in me screamed to fight back. To protect what remained of my dignity. Instead…I bowed my head.
Her expression shifted. Very slightly. Amusement.
I wanted to tell her I hated her. That my family abandoned me. That I never wanted this. That none of this was fair. Instead I whispered:
The red-haired ranger grabbed me by the collar. Dragged me backward. As the doors opened, I heard Hannah speak one final time.
I froze. She smiled from her throne-like chair.
Her eyes gleamed with something deeply unsettling.
"I may allow you to hold a real weapon."

The chamber erupted in quiet laughter. The doors slammed shut behind me. And somehow…I missed being punched. Because now I understood the truth. The women outside were wolves. Captain Hannah Icetear? She was the one who taught wolves how to hunt.

I would not escorted to noble quarters. This realization struck me long before I saw where I would be sleeping. The red-haired ranger dragged me through the upper halls of the garrison by the back of my collar like a misbehaving dog. My boots scraped against old wooden floors.
Every passing ranger stared. Some laughed. Others whispered. A few simply looked disappointed that I was still alive. One silver-haired elf muttered:
I kept my mouth shut. For once. Growth. Painful, humiliating growth.
The ranger stopped outside Captain Hannah's private chambers. Massive carved doors stood guarded by two silent sentries.
For one stupid moment, I thought perhaps Hannah had shown mercy. Perhaps I would be stationed nearby because of my title. Perhaps…

The ranger opened a tiny side door beside Hannah's chamber. My optimism died instantly. It was a storage closet. A very small storage closet. She threw me inside. I crashed into buckets, cloths, and cleaning supplies. Something sharp stabbed my ribs.
The ranger leaned against the doorway smiling.
Her smile disappeared. She stepped forward.

She pointed. In the corner sat a thin mattress. If one could call it that. It looked older than some kingdoms. Stained. Sunken. Mold creeping across one side. It rested beside mops, soap buckets, and old weapon-cleaning oil. Above it was a tiny barred window no wider than my forearm. Cold wind seeped through the cracks.
The ranger tossed my bag at me.
Then she slammed the door shut. Darkness swallowed me. I sat there for a long time. Listening. The camp never truly slept. Metal clashed somewhere in the distance. Women shouted battle chants.

Horses screamed. Someone was singing. No...not singing. It sounded ritualistic. Like mourning. But there was no sadness in it. Only rage. The sound rose through the forest like ancient ghosts crying for war. Then came drums. Slow. Violent. Relentless.
I wrapped myself in my coat and lay on the mattress. The smell nearly made me vomit. Mold. Sweat. Blood. Rotting leather.

I stared at the ceiling. My brothers were likely sleeping in warm beds right now. My father probably sat near a fireplace drinking expensive wine. My mother likely told guests how honorable this arrangement was. How proud she was.
I laughed bitterly into the darkness. Then whispered, thinking of the company I had to keep for the next several months.
Silence. Then..the door creaked open. I sat upright.

Three red-cloaked rangers entered. Their movements were uneven. Drunk. The smell of ale hit me immediately. One kicked the door shut behind her. The tallest one crouched in front of me. She smiled. And I realized drunken elves somehow looked even more dangerous.
She punched me across the mouth.
My head slammed against the wall. Blood filled my mouth.
The second elf picked up one of my books from my bag. She laughed at the title.
She tossed it into a dirty bucket of water. The third one leaned against the wall watching. Too calm. That one frightened me most. The tall elf grabbed my shirt.
I remained silent. She punched me again.
That one landed so hard I saw white.
"I didn't fight at Ashwinter," I gasped.

She threw me onto the floor. All three began kicking me. Ribs. Back. Stomach. Legs. I curled into myself. They kept going. I tried covering my face. A boot crushed my hand. I screamed. One grabbed my hair and pulled my head up.
"You wear noble silk while our dead rot in ash."
She slammed my face into the floorboards. I tasted blood and splintered wood. Something inside me snapped. I swung wildly. My fist connected with someone's jaw.
The room froze. All three stared at me. I had made a catastrophic mistake. The calm one smiled.
The beating became much worse. Boots. Fists. Elbows. Someone slammed my ribs with a wooden stool. I screamed until screaming became impossible. My vision blurred.
The final thing I remember…was one of them kneeling beside me. She gently brushed hair from my forehead. Almost tender. Then she whispered.
And struck me across the temple. Darkness consumed everything.
I awoke choking on the taste of dried blood.

For several long seconds, I did not know where I was. My cheek rested against damp stone. My body felt shattered. Then memory returned all at once. The closet. The drunken rangers. The fists. The boots. The laughter.

I groaned as I rolled onto my back. Pain immediately erupted through my ribs. One of them had kicked me repeatedly there after I stopped fighting. Another had struck my jaw until I tasted blood. And the final blow...I touched the back of my skull and hissed. Still swollen. Still wet with dried blood. Wonderful. What a glorious diplomatic exchange between nations.

I attempted to sit up and nearly blacked out. The tiny chamber spun violently. The room they had thrown me into was hardly a room at all. It was a narrow storage closet beside Captain Hannahrial Icetear's private chambers. A rotting mattress sat in one corner. Buckets. Mops. Cleaning chemicals. Old cloths stained black and brown. A tiny barred window let in cold grey morning light.
Rain tapped softly against stone. Then…
The door flew open. I flinched so hard pain shot through my ribs. A tall red-haired ranger stood there. She looked disgusted to see I was still alive.
Her eyes narrowed. She stepped forward and kicked my mattress. Hard.
"You have exactly four minutes to bring High-Captain Hannarial's breakfast."
Her expression slowly became murderous. Then deeply amused.
She turned and shouted down the hallway.
Roaring laughter erupted somewhere outside. Multiple voices laughed. One woman nearly choked from how hard she was laughing.
The ranger leaned close to my face.
"The High-Captain eats every morning at first bell."
"If that tray is not on her desk before the final toll of the bell…"
"You'll wish last night had killed you."
She released me. I collapsed onto my knees.
The first bell echoed across Crimson Vale. A massive metallic sound. Deep. Ancient. Then a second smaller bell began counting downward. One. Two. Three..
I stumbled upright and ran. Barefoot. Bleeding. Half-conscious. Still wearing yesterday's ruined clothes.
I sprinted through the morning chaos of Crimson Vale. The camp was already alive.

Thousands of women moving with horrifying efficiency around me. Blades clashed in training yards. Archers practiced from elevated towers. Mounted ranger units rode toward Thorn Gate. Smiths hammered steel. Priestesses chanted near sacred fires.
Some rangers openly laughed as they watched me sprint by like a dying rat. One deliberately extended her foot. I tripped. My face slammed into mud. The surrounding women burst into laughter.
"I bet he cries before she breaks his fingers!"
I scrambled up and ran harder.

The Bloodroot Tavern stood near the central grounds. Massive. Loud. Already serving morning meals. I burst through the doors gasping for breath. The tavern instantly quieted. Dozens of red rangers stared.
A towering dark-haired tavern mistress stood behind the counter. Arms folded. Massive shoulders. Scar over one eye.
She stared. Then looked at a nearby clock mounted on the wall. Then back at me.
She slowly lifted a tray. Perfectly prepared. Black tea. Roasted venison. Fresh bread. Berries. Her expression became amused.
"She likes the berries on the left side."
I stared in horror. Sure enough, the berries were on the wrong side.
My hands shook violently as I rearranged the tray. Several nearby rangers laughed into their drinks. One yelled.
I ran. Second bell. Final toll. Echoing. Loud. Merciless.

I reached Hannah's command hall gasping for breath. I burst through the doors. And froze. Captain Hannah Icetear sat behind her desk. Perfectly composed. Perfectly dressed. Perfectly still. Two elite rangers stood beside her. The entire room was silent.
I stumbled forward. Placed the tray down. And looked up.
She slowly looked toward the large bronze clock mounted behind her. Then back at me.
She stood. Slowly. Quietly. That was somehow worse than shouting.
She stopped walking. The room became deathly silent. One ranger looked away. Wrong move. Hannah's gaze sharpened.
"You are speaking to me as though I care."
I immediately dropped to my knees.
She crouched before me. Her voice became almost gentle.
"If assassins poison me because my breakfast arrives late…"
She pressed a finger against my chest.
"If my blood sugar drops before command meetings…"
"If my schedule breaks because you are incompetent…"
"Why should I suffer for your weakness?"
Her hand shot forward. She grabbed my fingers. And bent one backward.
I screamed so loudly, birds erupted from nearby trees outside. White agony consumed my entire body. I collapsed onto the floor shaking. My finger bent at an unnatural angle. Tears flooded my eyes.
She sat down and began eating. As if nothing had happened. She took one bite. Paused. Looked at me.
"The berries are on the correct side."
I stared at her through tears.
Then she pointed toward the door.
I froze. The two rangers began laughing. One nearly fell over. Hannah continued eating calmly.
She looked at my unbroken hand.

I crawled out of the chamber trying not to vomit. Behind me, Crimson Vale continued its morning routine. Perfectly. Brutally. On time. And for the first time since arriving, I began to understand. This place was not chaos. It was discipline sharpened into cruelty. And I was trapped inside its clockwork teeth.
My finger throbbed with every heartbeat. It felt alive. Angry. Punishing. The crude splint placed around it by the camp medic looked less like medical treatment and more like a threat made from wood.

I sat alone behind the Bloodroot Tavern. Rainwater dripped from wooden rooftops. My stomach twisted violently. I had not eaten since arriving at Crimson Vale. Not properly. Not unless one counted being punched in the face as nourishment. Which, admittedly, the elves seemed to.
I stared at the tray prepared for Captain Hannah's midday meal. Perfect roasted pheasant. Steamed vegetables. Fresh dark bread. Honey-glazed fruits. And a small silver cup of wine.

My stomach growled so loudly one of the nearby tavern maids laughed. Pathetic. I looked around. No one seemed to be paying attention. The kitchen workers were busy. Rangers shouted across the tavern. Steel mugs slammed against tables. No one was watching me. At least...I thought no one was watching me. Did they even care if I starved, they didn't offer me anything at all.
I stared at the roasted pheasant. Then at my shaking hands. Then back at the pheasant.

I tore off a tiny piece. Then another. Then another. Warm juices filled my mouth. I nearly cried. It tasted better than anything I had ever eaten. Starvation turns even stolen scraps into divine miracles. I swallowed quickly. Then drank a tiny sip from her wine. Just enough to be petty. Just enough to feel victorious.
I carefully adjusted the food. Moved vegetables around. Rotated the pheasant slightly. Perfect. No one would know. I smiled for the first time since arriving. A dangerous mistake.
I arrived outside Hannah's chamber precisely on time. This time early, even. I smirked to myself. Learned my lesson, to handle these beasts. I entered.
Captain Hannah sat reviewing military reports. She didn't look up.
I obeyed. She continued reading. Took her fork. Cut into the pheasant. Then paused.
Slowly…very slowly, she lifted the fork. Examined the meat. Then set it down. She sniffed the wine. Then looked at me.
"There are exactly seven kitchen staff who prepare my meals."
"And one obsessive tavern mistress who arranges portions identically every day."
She now stood inches from me.
She grabbed my broken finger. Hard. I screamed instantly.
She squeezed harder. I nearly blacked out.
She released me. I collapsed to my knees screaming. The room echoed with my breathing.
Hannah crouched before me. And for the first time…she looked almost curious.
I hesitated. And made the catastrophic mistake of telling the truth.
Her expression changed instantly. Back to cold amusement.
She rang a small silver bell. The door opened instantly. Two female rangers entered.
No one answered. That was somehow worse. Just dragged violently.

The Rain Hall was enormous. Ancient stone. Towering carved pillars. Steam rising from warm pools. And above, an enchanted ceiling that endlessly poured soft rainfall into the chamber. Hundreds of female rangers bathed openly. Talking. Laughing. Relaxing.
Then they saw me. Silence spread. I was pulled forward. Humiliation burned through me.
Hannah entered behind us. Calm. Elegant. Terrifying. She addressed the entire hall.
"This human stole from his commanding officer."
The hall erupted in laughter. I wanted death. Hannah pointed to the wet stone floor.
I stared at the endless massive chamber.
The entire hall burst into cruel laughter.

And that night, while the beating rain fell endlessly from the ceiling. While elite elven assassins bathed around me. While they mocked me, splashed me, kicked soap toward my face..I scrubbed. And scrubbed. And scrubbed. Hungry. Humiliated. Broken. And hating Hannah Icetear more than I had ever hated anyone in my life.

I dreamt of home. Not the grand halls. Not noble banquets. Not my father's political dinners. I dreamt of something smaller. My mother sitting beside the garden fountain at dusk. Bare feet touching the water. Reading quietly while fireflies floated above the hedges.

When I was younger, I used to hide behind the statues and steal the honey cakes she kept beside her tea. She always pretended not to notice. Always. Even when crumbs covered my face. Even when I was terrible at lying.
She would simply smile and say.
"One day your greed will make you suffer, Alfar."
I used to laugh when she said it. Then someone kicked my ribs. And I awoke screaming. The dream shattered. Reality returned. Cold. Pain. Darkness.
My closet room smelled of mildew and old blood. My broken finger pulsed inside its splint. My shoulders screamed from scrubbing the Rain Hall floors.

My stomach twisted from the small meal I had been given before collapsing. I barely remembered eating. A bowl of venison stew. Hard bread. A cup of bitter herbal water. Then sleep had claimed me like drowning.

I vaguely remembered waking once in the night. Hands dragging me from the mattress. Laughter. Not drunken this time. Almost ceremonial. A ring of female Rangers standing around me in the courtyard beneath moonlight. My arms tied. My knees forced into wet dirt. One by one they struck me. Not hard enough to cripple. Not soft enough to ignore. Open palms. Wooden rods. Whips. A ritual. Each woman stepped forward. Delivered one strike. Then stepped back. No screaming. No chaos. Only discipline.
One of them whispered into my ear afterward.
And now..morning. And another boot in my ribs. I groaned.

That voice. Cold. Controlled. Female. I opened swollen eyes. Hannah stood above me. Golden hair tied back for training. White and red armor gleaming in faint morning light. She looked immaculate. I looked like something dug from a grave.
She tossed a bucket of freezing water onto me. I convulsed. The cold punched the breath from my lungs.
She smiled. That smile always made things worse.

The Silent Yard was already full. Hundreds of Rangers surrounded the massive northern training grounds. Watching. Waiting. Betting. I could hear coins exchanging hands. Wonderful. I had become gambling entertainment.

The training grounds themselves were enormous. Mud arenas with patches of frost clusters. Archery towers. Weapon racks. Execution platforms. Burn pits. Massive beast cages. And at the center. Me. Half-dead. Barely standing. Holding a wooden sword.
Hannah stood beside me like judgment made flesh. She raised one hand. The crowd quieted immediately. That terrified me more than shouting.
One by one they stepped forward.
"Virelyn Shadebloom. The Shadow Captain." Built like war itself. White hair. Scarred skin. Eyes full of contempt. She looked at me like weak meat.
"Caeleira Duskfall. The Bow Captain." Beautiful. Silent. Moonlit eyes. She looked as though she could shoot my heartbeat from my chest.
Shaedra Nyxthorn. The Blade Captain." If sadism wore a face, it's her. Golden skin with tattoos scarred in spiral patterns.
'Thalara Vintshade. The Chef." Her pale hands were stained red. I suddenly did not want to know what was in breakfast stew.
"Syrel Thorneheart. The Medic." She waved her bone needle at me cheerfully. Monster.
"The Twins. Rellien and Vessa." They smiled at exactly the same time. I nearly vomited.
"Solenyra Gravespine. The High-Warden." Even standing still, she felt larger than everyone. Her single glowing eye settled on me.
"You should pray she returns in a merciful mood."
Hannah tossed me a wooden blade. It hit my chest and fell into the mud.
I laughed. Not because it was funny. Because my mind broke briefly.

She moved. Pain exploded across my face. The wooden sword struck my jaw so hard I spun sideways. Blood hit the dirt. The crowd roared. I stumbled upright. She hit me again. And again. And again. Every strike is precise. Never wasted. My wrist. My ribs. My knee. My shoulder.

I swung wildly. Missed every time. She moved like cold water. Beautiful. Precise. Cruel. I fell. Rose. Fell again. At one point I crawled toward my sword through mud while the crowd laughed so hard some could barely breathe.
By the end, I could no longer lift my arms. Hannah pressed her wooden blade beneath my chin.

The crowd erupted. And then she entered. Shaedra Nyxthorn looked like violence given a body. Golden skin. Tattooed arms. Twin curved blades. A smile too joyful for someone holding weapons. She bowed dramatically.

Six Rangers dragged in a chained ogre. Massive. Foaming. Screaming. Its wrists were bound in iron. Its face covered in scars. It looked at the Rangers with pure hatred. Then it looked at me. And somehow I understood that feeling.
The chains dropped. The ogre charged. Shaedra laughed. Not nervous laughter. Not battle rage. Joy. Pure joy. She moved. The ogre screamed. Its tendons opened first. Then its eyes. Then its stomach.
She danced around it while it bled. Sometimes stepping back simply to watch it panic. She could have killed it immediately. She chose not to. The crowd screamed her name.
The ogre collapsed. Begging. Crying. Trying to crawl. Shaedra crouched beside it and gently stroked its face. Then slit its throat.
Blood pooled into the dirt. My stomach turned. Shaedra slowly looked at me. Blood dripping from her blades. Waiting.
And because my mouth is apparently possessed by suicidal spirits..I whispered..
Silence swallowed the yard. Every Ranger turned toward me. Shaedra tilted her head. Then began laughing. Slowly. Softly. That somehow felt worse than anger. She pointed one bloody blade at me.
The Rangers erupted into laughter, and yelled out:
My legs gave out beneath me. Mud swallowed my knees.
Shaedra crouched before me. Far too close. Her golden skin was splattered with blood. Her tattooed arms flexed as she tilted my chin upward with her blade.
"You know what I do to little noble princes?"

A war horn split the air. Deep. Violent. Ancient. Another horn answered from afar. Then bells began ringing violently across Crimson Vale. The entire training yard froze. Every Ranger turned toward the eastern walls.
A scout sprinted into the field, covered in blood and mud. She dropped to one knee before Hannah.

The atmosphere changed instantly. Mockery vanished. Now they looked like soldiers again. Real ones. Archers moved. Mounted Rangers ran for their horses. Blade units armed themselves. The scout swallowed.
Shaedra looked at me one final time. Her smile was almost affectionate. Which somehow made it worse.
Then she and her squad sprinted toward the eastern gate. And that should have been the end of my suffering for the day. Naturally. It wasn't.
Seconds later, the great northern gate, "Icetear Gate".. Opened. Massive wooden doors groaned apart. Several mounted Rangers entered the camp. Silent. Disciplined. Their armor was dusted with frost.

At their center rode a woman dressed in blackened silver armor and crimson cloth. She dismounted slowly. And the entire courtyard changed. Veteran Rangers straightened. Conversations stopped. Even the loudest soldiers lowered their voices.

She was tall. Elegant. Terrifyingly composed. Long raven-black hair fell straight down her back like spilled ink. Her face was beautiful in the way winter lakes looked beautiful. Still. Cold. And dangerous if you stepped too far. Her green eyes moved across the training grounds.

The dead ogre. The blood. The broken weapons. Then finally..me. Half kneeling in mud. Covered in bruises. Breathing like a dying animal. Her expression didn't change. Which somehow felt worse than laughter.

She approached Hannah. The two women stared at one another for a moment. Something passed between them. Respect. Shared grief. Unspoken history. Then the black-haired woman finally spoke. Her voice was calm.
Her eyes drifted toward me again.
The woman studied me longer. I wished she wouldn't. I felt like prey being inspected by a panther that hadn't yet decided if it was hungry.
I attempted to stand. Immediately failed. Wonderful. Her eyebrow lifted slightly. That tiny reaction somehow humiliated me more than Shaedra's words ever had. I forced out the words.
Several nearby Rangers looked horrified that I had spoken. The woman stared at me. Then, unexpectedly…she smiled. It wasn't warm. It wasn't cruel. It was simply amused.
My stomach dropped. Of course. Because apparently one terrifying Icetear woman was not enough for my miserable existence.
Anthuriun leaned slightly closer. Her voice lowered.
"I heard you called Shaedra a wild beast."
I said nothing. Her smile widened.

Another horn echoed from the eastern walls. Anthuriun turned calmly toward the chaos. Then looked back at me one final time. And for the first time all day..I met an elf whose cruelty seemed quieter. More intelligent. And somehow far more dangerous.
"I think I'll keep an eye on you, little human."
And somehow…that felt like the worst news I had received all week. Which was impressive. Because my week had been catastrophic.

Victory has a smell. I learned that the night the "Thorn Gate" and the eastern walls held. It smelled like burning troll flesh. Like blood steaming on cold iron. Like ale spilled across ancient wood. Like sweat, smoke, and celebration from women who had spent their evening carving living creatures apart and now wished to reward themselves for it.

By the time the gates were secured, the sun had long vanished behind the black trees of Crimson Vale. The returning Rangers came in waves. Some laughing. Some carrying severed troll heads by their hair. Some dragging broken weapons. Some limping. Some bleeding. None complaining. They moved through the camp like returning goddesses of war.

The entire fortress seemed alive. Torches blazed brighter. War drums echoed. Songs in ancient elvish rose from the tavern district. Not beautiful songs. Violent ones. Songs that sounded like sharpened teeth.
I stood outside Hannah's chambers holding my bruised ribs and trying not to vomit.
Her door swung open. Captain Hannah emerged fully armored, her blonde hair damp from a fresh wash, now braided loosely over one shoulder. Her green eyes found me instantly.
I hated how my body reacted before my mind did. I straightened. Stood taller. Fear trained faster than discipline.
I stared at her. She stared back. Neither of us smiled. She handed me a carved metal tray.
Her eyes drifted toward my bruised fingers.
Then she walked away. Just like that. As if threatening permanent bodily damage was ordinary conversation. Which, unfortunately…here, it was.
The tavern was called "The Bloodroot Hall". Naturally. Because apparently naming a tavern something normal like The Silver Cup would kill these women.

The moment I entered, sound assaulted me. Roaring laughter. Shouting. Tables shaking. Mugs slamming. Songs screamed in ancient elvish. Rangers danced on tables. Others arm-wrestled. One woman was being stitched up while drinking. Another was showing off a troll ear necklace she had apparently made less than an hour ago.
Several heads turned toward me. And the laughter changed. It became sharper. Focused. Predatory.
I said it loudly toward the kitchen.
The chef, Thalara Vintshade, silently nodded from behind hanging cuts of meat. She began plating the meal. I nearly cried from relief.
Then someone kicked the back of my knees. I hit the floor hard. Laughter erupted. I didn't need to look up. I already knew. Shaedra Nyxthorn.
Her boots stepped into view. Slow. Deliberate. She crouched in front of me. Golden skin. Tattooed arms. Predatory smile. Eyes that belonged to something raised incorrectly by civilization.
"I need Captain Hannah's dinner." I whisper.
The room laughed. Shaedra looked offended.
She stood. Grabbed my hair. Dragged me across the tavern floor. My tray clattered away. I screamed. Nobody moved to help. Of course they didn't.
She dragged me toward a massive iron clock mounted on the tavern wall. Its hands ticked loudly. Mockingly. She forced me onto my knees.
I looked. The clock. Nine minutes until Hannah's dinner deadline.
She smiled wider. Then forced my face toward the clock.
Minute hand moved. The tavern roared with laughter. Another minute. Then another. My pulse became violent.
The final minute passed. The clock hand moved. Late. The tavern exploded with laughter. Shaedra released me.
I sprinted. Grabbed the dinner plate. Ran through rain-soaked pathways. Slipped twice. Nearly dropped the tray.
Burst through Hannah's chambers. She was seated at her table. Waiting. Perfect posture. Perfect silence. Perfect rage. I was shaking.
She looked at the clock. Then at me. Then at the slightly ruined dinner tray. Then back at me.
I hesitated. And made the worst possible choice. I told the truth.
Silence. Hannah stood. For one beautiful second I thought she might defend me. Then she walked toward me. Hope is such a stupid thing.
She grabbed my injured hand. And drove a dagger between my fingers into the wooden table. I screamed. The blade stopped millimeters from bone. Food scattered everywhere.
"You allowed another Ranger to control your task."
She yanked the dagger free. I collapsed. Bleeding. Shaking. She sat back down.
I stared at her. She stared back.

By the time midnight arrived, I was barely conscious. I dragged myself into my tiny closet beside Hannah's chambers. My mattress smelled like mold. My hands trembled. Every muscle screamed. I collapsed face-first. Still wearing blood-soaked clothing. I didn't even remove my boots. Sleep hit me instantly.
Then…someone was already sitting in the corner. I froze. Moonlight touched her smile. Shaedra.
She sat casually in my tiny room. Like a demon waiting beside a deathbed.
She stood. Slowly. Her head nearly touched the ceiling.
She crouched in front of me. Every inch of her radiated danger.
Silence. Then Shaedra laughed, so hard she nearly fell backward. Actually laughed. Tears formed in her eyes. Eventually she leaned close enough for me to smell blood and ale on her breath.
"That is the funniest thing you've ever said."
The door opened behind her. I looked. Relief exploded through me. Hannah stood there. Thank the gods. Thank the…
Hannah looked irritated. Not protective. Not shocked. I stared at her.
Hannah looked at Shaedra. Then at me. Then sighed.
I looked between both women in disbelief. Rain hammered softly against the tiny barred window.
And shut the door. The lock clicked. I stared at it. Frozen. Surely…surely she would come back. Surely this was another joke. Another lesson. Another cruel scare tactic.
Nothing. I rushed forward and pounded against the door.
"Please don't leave me here with her!"

Nothing. Not even footsteps. Just silence. The kind of silence that confirmed everything. She had truly left. My fists slowly stopped moving. My forehead rested against the cold wood. My breathing shook violently. Then even that began to slow. Something inside me simply…went quiet. Not peace. Something worse. The realization that resistance had become meaningless.

I turned slowly. Shaedra remained seated on my mattress. Watching. Patient. Like she had always known this moment would come. Her cruel smile had softened into something almost tender. Which somehow terrified me more.

I stared at her. My body ached. My hand throbbed. My ribs burned. My face still carried bruises from training. My mind felt hollow. I had nothing left. No threats. No pride. No anger. Even hatred required energy I no longer possessed.
My voice emerged as little more than a whisper.
I hated how small I sounded.
Her expression changed. For the first time…she looked genuinely surprised. Then slowly, she opened her arms. Cruel. Inviting. Possessive. Like a wolf welcoming wounded prey into its jaws.

I stood motionless for several seconds. Every instinct screamed at me to run. There was nowhere to go. No one was coming. Not Hannah. Not my family. Not the gods. Just her. My legs moved before my pride could stop them. One weak step. Then another. Then another. Until I stood before her. I looked utterly broken.
I closed my eyes. And in complete exhaustion…in humiliating, defeated meekness..I slowly collapsed into Shaedra Nyxthorn's waiting embrace.

Her arms wrapped around me instantly. Strong. Warm. Terrible. One hand moved into my hair. The other pressed firmly against my back. Holding me there. Claiming me. And as sleep deprivation, pain, fear, and humiliation finally crushed what little strength remained..I began to cry.
Quietly. Pathetically. Into the chest of the woman I hated most. Shaedra leaned down to my ear. And whispered softly…
Darkness took me soon after. And I hated myself most of all for how safe that monster's arms briefly felt.

Pain becomes easier to predict. That was the lie I told myself three weeks after Shaedra claimed my nights. That if enough suffering repeated itself in recognizable patterns, then perhaps the human mind could adapt.
Morning humiliation. Midday labor. Evening terror. Nighttime uncertainty. A schedule. A rhythm. A civilized arrangement for barbarism. How comforting.

By then my body had become a map of Crimson Vale's affection. Purple bruises from Hannah. Rib pain from training. Bite scars of cold rain. Cuts from labor. Hand wounds from kitchen accidents. And the fresh bruises around my throat from Shaedra's "playful" nightly visits.
I had stopped looking in mirrors. Not out of vanity. Out of self-preservation. I preferred remembering my face as it once was.

That morning began in the southern training yard. Which was already a terrible sign. Rain drizzled lightly over the massive open grounds of Crimson Vale. Archers trained on moving targets. Mounted Rangers raced through obstacle courses. Shadow Casters practiced controlled energy detonations near the western cliffs. And in the center training pit. Stood the twins.

Rellien and Vessa Aerwyn. Supervisors of the cleaning corps. Though calling them cleaners felt dishonest. Executioners who occasionally held mops was more accurate. They stood perfectly still. Silver braided hair. Matching expressions. Matching weapons. Matching smiles that never reached their eyes. They even spoke in broken synchronized fragments.
The surrounding Rangers laughed. Wonderful. I picked up a wooden blade at my feet. Vessa frowned.
Rellien tossed me real steel. I barely caught it.

Then they attacked. Together. Perfectly synchronized. They moved like mirrored nightmares. One low. One high. One feint. One strike. I barely defended the first ten seconds before panic replaced technique. Weeks of training gone..For the fear of being cut.
Steel screamed. Mud splashed. The crowd cheered every time I stumbled. Then I made a mistake. A small one. My blade slipped. Vessa smiled. Rellien whispered…

Then agony exploded through my arm. I screamed. My sword dropped. I stared in horror. A deep slash ran from wrist to elbow. Long. Open. Blood poured down my fingers. I collapsed into the mud. The twins stepped back calmly.
The crowd laughed. One Ranger yelled…
"Take him to Syrel before he leaks out!"
They carried me into "The Quiet Mercy" after I nearly fainted from blood loss. That was what the carved wooden sign above the infirmary entrance called it.
I laughed when I read it. Not because it was funny. Because blood loss had made me delirious. Then I was dragged inside. And heard screaming. My laughter stopped.

The interior looked less like a place of healing and more like a butcher's chapel. Black stone walls. Hanging herbs. Rows of polished surgical tools. Glass jars containing things I did not want identified. Blood gutters carved into the floor.

Everywhere..Rangers waiting calmly for their turn. One woman sat with an arrow lodged through her shoulder, drinking ale. Another calmly held her own severed fingertip wrapped in cloth. A third had half her face burned. She was smiling. Why was she smiling? Then I saw why.

At the center of the room stood Syrel Thorneheart, and her familiar attendants. She was beautiful in an unnatural way. Silver-white hair. Pale skin threaded faintly with visible blue veins. Soft lips. Gentle eyes. The kind face of someone you would trust instantly. Which made what she was doing infinitely worse.

She was stitching a Ranger's abdomen. The woman on the table was awake. No restraints. No sedatives. Just a leather strap between her teeth. Syrel hummed softly while threading flesh back together. Like she was sewing a dress. The Ranger screamed. Syrel frowned.
I tried to leave. A hand shoved me forward.
I looked at my arm. Blood was pouring onto the stone floor.
Syrel looked up. Her pale eyes met mine. And she smiled warmly.
That somehow felt more threatening than Hannah screaming at me.
I was pushed onto the stone slab. Cold stone met my skin. I immediately tried sitting up again. Syrel gently pressed my chest. And somehow forced me back down with shocking strength.
Her voice was barely above a whisper. I froze. She lifted my arm carefully. Studied the wound. Her fingers were warm. Unexpectedly soft.
Her fingers pressed deeper into the wound. I screamed.
Then she picked up the bone needle. I stared at it. It looked ancient. Carved. Almost ceremonial.
She leaned closer. Close enough for me to smell lavender on her skin. Close enough to mistake her for kind.

Then she drove the needle into my flesh. The world disappeared. My scream tore itself from my lungs. My entire body lurched upward..and her hand immediately moved into my hair. Firm. Holding my head against her chest. Not cruel. Not comforting. Something horrifyingly in between.
I trembled violently. She continued stitching. Each puncture sent lightning through my arm. I cried openly now. Too broken to care. And through all of it…she kept speaking softly into my hair.
When she finished, I collapsed. Completely limp. Tears soaked my face. I could barely think.
My soul left my body. She gently rolled me onto my stomach.

She climbed onto the slab and straddled me from behind. And suddenly her fingers dug into my shoulders. I screamed. She pressed harder. Finding bruises. Hidden knots. Deep injuries I hadn't even noticed. Every time I relaxed…the pressure became soothing. Then suddenly painful again. Then soothing. Then painful. My body didn't know whether to fight or melt.
She pressed into my lower back. I nearly blacked out.
Another pressure point. I screamed into the stone.
Her fingers moved near my ribs.
When she finally let me go…I couldn't stand. She helped me sit upright. Almost gently. I stared at her. Terrified.
For once..she became quiet. No smile. No games.
She looked toward the rain outside.
"My younger sister died on a table exactly like this one."
She looked back at me. Her softness returned. Which now terrified me even more.
She tucked a loose strand of hair behind my ear. Almost affectionately.
"…I may occasionally enjoy making noble sons cry."
Then she kissed my forehead. Like a nurse soothing a child. And whispered…
I stared at her in horror.
I looked at my fresh wound.
"We'll see if your skin deserves to keep them."
I considered cutting my own arm off before sunrise.

Not because I wanted to die. That would have been dramatic. And unfortunately, I was far too exhausted for drama. It simply seemed mathematically preferable to returning to Syrel Thorneheart. One missing arm felt like a reasonable trade.
I lay awake on my mold-infested mattress beside Hannah's chambers, staring at the damp ceiling while rain tapped softly against the tiny barred window.

My stitched arm throbbed with every heartbeat. Not sharp pain. Worse. A slow pulling sensation. Like my skin was being reminded it had been violated. And every time I drifted toward sleep. I remembered Syrel's lips brushing my forehead.
That soft whisper. Return tomorrow. Like a lover scheduling another date. Absolutely revolting.
By dawn, I had convinced myself I would not go.
Then Hannah kicked my mattress. Hard. I rolled off it and hit the floor. She stood above me fully dressed for training. Long blonde hair braided. Armor polished. Beautiful as divine judgment.
"She said she wanted to remove the stitches."
Hannah crouched in front of me. For one fleeting moment, I thought sympathy might appear. Instead she adjusted the collar of my ruined shirt.
And I hated how relieved I felt that she hadn't personally dragged me there. Growth.
The walk to The Quiet Mercy felt longer than usual.

Rangers trained all around me. Some waved. Some laughed. A few asked if I was "visiting my silver-haired lover." One offered betting odds on whether I would scream louder today. Community truly is beautiful.
When I reached the infirmary doors, I stopped. The screaming had already started inside. That must have been a bad one. I nearly turned around. Then the door opened.
Syrel stood there. As though she had been waiting. Silver hair tied loosely. Fresh red stains on her apron. Soft smile.
That word should not sound so intimate from someone holding surgical scissors.

The infirmary was quieter today. Not peaceful. Never peaceful. Just quieter. The screaming ranger from before was passed out on a stone slab, missing her arm. One of the familiar attendants were enchanting the fresh stitches.

Rain tapped against the windows. Herbs burned in hanging metal bowls. The smell was strangely calming. Until I noticed another Ranger missing two fingers calmly drinking tea in the corner. Perspective is cruel.
Syrel led me to the same stone slab from yesterday. I stopped.
"Because last time you nearly tore my soul from my body."
She smiled faintly. Then surprised me by sitting in a chair instead.
Suspiciously easy. Which meant this was likely worse.
I sat. She gently took my arm. Unwrapped the bandages. I hissed immediately. The wound looked ugly. Red. Angry. Stitched tightly.
Syrel studied it quietly. Then looked disappointed.

Then she began cleaning the wound. Slowly. Far gentler than yesterday. That somehow unnerved me more. Her fingers traced my forearm carefully. Applying herbs. Cleaning dried blood. I found myself watching her.
She tied fresh bandages. Then leaned against the table beside me. For once, she wasn't working. Just…existing. That alone felt intimate. Dangerously so.
I went still. Her gaze drifted toward the rain outside.
"Do you know how many survived Ashwinter from House Icetear?"
"Her brothers. Her sisters. Cousins. Friends. Entire bloodlines vanished in one campaign."
"Anthuriun was young. She watched her mother & youngest sister die."
"She survived by hiding beneath their dead bodies."
Silence wrapped around us. Rain continued outside.
"But war gave her permission to become honest."
Her fingers absentmindedly adjusted my bandages.
"I found what remained of her bracelet."
Silence again. Then she looked at me. Soft. Terrifyingly soft.
"You are not hated because of who you are, Alfar."
That was the first time someone here used my name gently.
"You are hated because you arrived carrying symbols of people who left graves behind."
"Hannah investigated your family before you arrived."
"She knew exactly who was being sent."
"To determine whether killing you would restart the war."
"She discovered your father is unusually honorable. Your mother is beloved by some of my people."
"She funded refugee shelters after the war. There is something different about her."
I stared at her. I had never known that. Syrel stepped closer.
That truth struck somewhere painfully deep.
Then Syrel lightly tapped my stitched arm. I flinched.
I stared at her in horror.
She leaned close enough for her lips to brush my ear.
Her fingers gently pinned my wrist to the table.
And somewhere deep inside me, I realized that terrified me more than her needle ever could.

I carried Hannah's dinner with both hands. Not because it was heavy, but because my fingers still remembered her. The tray trembled slightly as I walked. Every step sent a dull pulse through my hand, through the nail that had not yet healed, through the memory of pressure, of control. I tried to steady it. Tried to slow my breathing. Tried to arrive before she noticed.
I was late. I knew it before I reached the door. The guards did not stop me. They never did. I stepped inside.
The tray slipped slightly in my grip as I bowed my head.
Her hand moved. Fast. Precise. She didn't strike my face. She took my hand. The injured one. And pressed. Not crushing. Not yet. Just enough.
Pain flared instantly, sharp and bright, climbing up my arm like fire. I bit down on the inside of my cheek so hard I tasted blood.
Her voice was calm. Worse than anger. My knees almost gave.

Her fingers tightened. Not enough to break. Enough to remind. A sound escaped me before I could stop it. Soft. Humiliating. She watched me. Measured the reaction. Then released. I staggered slightly, catching the tray before it fell.
I did. Carefully. My hand shook violently now. I kept my head lowered. Didn't look at her. Didn't dare. She didn't speak again. Didn't acknowledge me. Didn't dismiss me.
I stood there anyway. Like something waiting to be told what it was allowed to be. Then I turned. And left.

The corridor felt colder on the way back. Quieter. Every sound sharper. Every step heavier. My hand throbbed with every heartbeat. But that wasn't what followed me. It was her silence. That always lingered longer than pain.
By the time I reached my room, I was hollow. Not exhausted. Empty. I closed the door. Locked it. Leaned against it. And let out a breath that shook on the way out.
My bag lay in the corner. Where I had left it. Where I had forgotten it. Where I had forgotten… myself. I stared at it for a long time. Then moved.
Slowly. Kneeling. Opening it. Clothes. Stiff with dried blood. A broken clasp. Fragments of a life that didn't exist anymore. My hand moved through it without thinking. Without care.

Until..paper, beside a satchel of gems & jewelry my uncle gave me to sell, if I ran short of coins. My fingers hovered over the letter. Then slowly lifted it out. Crumpled. Folded deep. Forgotten. My breath caught. Because I saw it before I opened it.
The name. Written across the front. "To High-Captain Hannariel."
My chest tightened. My hands began to shake again, worse than before. This wasn't pain. This was something else. I shouldn't read this. I knew that.
Knew it the same way I knew disobedience had consequences. The same way I knew Syrel's hands could be gentle… and still destroy me.
The paper crackled softly, too loud in the silence. My eyes moved over the words slowly. Not reading. Recognizing. My mother's hand. Her voice. Her tone.

Then..a name. Serenus Icetear. Everything stopped. The room. The air. My breath. Serenus. Icetear. I read it again. Slower. As if that would change it. It didn't. My mother's father…My grandfather….An Icetear?
My vision blurred. My grip tightened on the paper. My entire body went cold. Hannariel. The letter slipped slightly in my hand. I caught it. Barely.
It came out small. Broken. My mind tried to reject it. Push it away. Make it something else. It couldn't. Bloodline. Family. Connection. I wasn't just a human.

Not here. Not to them. Elu-dues. The word rose in my mind like something poisonous. I stood up too quickly. The room tilted. My breath came faster. Shallow. Wrong. I needed to give this to her. Now. Before..before what? Before it got worse? It was already worse.
I moved toward the door, the letter clutched in my hand, my heart pounding so loudly I could hear it.
The handle turned. I froze. The door opened. Shaedra stepped inside. I didn't think. I reacted. The letter disappeared into the bag. Buried. Hidden. Gone.
Her eyes flicked briefly toward the movement. Then back to me. Slowly. Smiling.
I said nothing. I couldn't. My chest still tight from the letter. My mind still reeling. She closed the door behind her. Locked it. The sound was deliberate. Measured.
Her gaze stayed on me as she moved. Unhurried. Certain. Like she already knew how this would end.
She stepped closer. Each step quiet. Controlled.
The lie came out too fast. Too thin. Her smile deepened.
She reached for me. Not roughly. Not yet. Her fingers brushed my shoulder. Light. Testing.
Her hand slid away. She turned casually, as if the room belonged to her. As if I did.

She began unfastening her armor. Slowly. Piece by piece. Not for display. Not for me. For comfort. Leather loosened. Straps fell. Steel set aside with soft, controlled movements. Until only silk remained. Dark. Clinging. Effortless.
She exhaled softly, settling into it. Then she looked back at me.
I didn't move. Not immediately. Her head tilted slightly. A warning.
I stepped forward. Slowly. The letter still burning in the back of my mind. The name still echoing. Hannariel. Icetear.
She watched me approach carefully, like she was reading something deeper than my face.
Her hand lifted. Rested lightly against my jaw. Not hurting. Not yet. But I understood. The letter would wait. It had to. Because in this place, truth didn't matter.
Only who stood in front of you. Only what they wanted. Only what they would take. And as her fingers tightened, just slightly..I let the truth sink back down. Buried. Hidden. Forgotten. For now.
Hannahrial did not look at me when I entered. That was how I knew something was wrong.
I stepped forward carefully, both hands steady beneath the tray, my breathing controlled, my eyes lowered. The chamber felt colder than usual. The air tighter.
She stood beside the table this time. Not by the window. Waiting.
I obeyed. One step. Two. Three. Close enough that I could feel her presence, not warmth, never warmth.. but pressure. Like standing too near a cliff edge.
I lowered the tray. My fingers trembled, just slightly.
She saw it. Her hand moved. Fast. She caught my wrist before I could pull away. The injured one. Her thumb pressed into the weak point between bone and tendon. Hard.
Pain surged up my arm, sharp enough to steal breath. My body folded instinctively, but I didn't pull away. I couldn't.
Pressure increased. My words died in my throat.
Not a question. A statement. Her eyes lifted slightly, not to meet mine, but to study my face from below my lowered gaze.
The words came out strained. Honest. Wrong.
Her grip tightened once more, just enough to remind me where I stood. Then she released me.
No dismissal gesture. No acknowledgment. Just that word. I left.

The East training grounds were colder. The Thorn Gate loomed overhead, dark wood reinforced with black iron, its edges wrapped in creeping, deadened vines hardened into jagged shapes. The walls beside it were worse. Thick with thorn growth, twisted and reinforced until they looked like something alive that had been forced to hold still.
This place didn't feel like a training ground. It felt like something that swallowed mistakes.
Shaedra was already there. Waiting. Of course she was.
She didn't greet me. Didn't speak.
She simply watched as I approached, her arms folded loosely, her posture relaxed in a way that made everything else feel tense.
It wasn't Hannah's tone. It was worse. Because there was amusement in it.
She stepped forward. Close. Too close. Her fingers brushed under my jaw, tilting my head up slightly before I could react.
Her thumb traced lightly along my throat. Right over the marks. The ones she had left. My body tensed immediately. She felt it. Smiled.
Her voice was just loud enough to carry. Just enough. I didn't need to turn to know. Syrel was there. Watching.
Shaedra's hand lingered. Deliberate now. Her fingers pressing just slightly into the bruised skin at my throat, her touch light, but intentional. A display. Not for me. For her.
She stepped back. Blade drawn in a single smooth motion.
The first strike came fast. I barely caught it. Pain shot through my arm.
Again. She moved around me. Not just attacking..circling. Closing distance. Breaking it. Her blade correcting mine. Her body brushing mine as she passed. Too close. Every time.
Her breath brushed my ear. My grip faltered. Her blade tapped my ribs. Harder this time.
I forced myself to move. To follow. To react.
Her hand caught my wrist again. Guiding. Adjusting. But not letting go.
And then…closer. Her body aligned with mine as she corrected my stance. Her voice low. Measured.
Her fingers tightened slightly. Not painful. But not gentle either. Her thumb brushed again across my throat. Over the marks.
I flinched. Just slightly. That was enough. The air shifted.

Syrel's voice cut through everything. Cold. Sharp. We turned. She stood just inside the training ground now. No longer distant. No longer observing. Her eyes were on Shaedra. Not me. That made it worse.
Shaedra didn't move. Didn't release me immediately.
Syrel's gaze dropped briefly. To my throat. To the marks. Then back up.
Shaedra finally let go. Slowly. Deliberately.
Syrel stepped forward. One step. Then another.
The word was quiet. Certain. Her eyes flicked to me. Just once. Something passed through them. Something sharp. Something… hurt. Then it was gone.
I did. Immediately. Backing away. The moment I cleared the space..they moved.
Steel met steel. Fast. Precise. No wasted motion. No hesitation.
Syrel moved like something restrained. Every strike clean. Every step controlled.
Shaedra met her. Not with force. With intent. Every movement grounded. Deliberate.

They didn't fight like enemies. They fought like equals. That was the problem. Blow for blow. Step for step. Neither yielding. Neither gaining. The sound of steel rang against the Thorn walls. Echoing. Sharp.
I stood frozen. Watching. Trying to understand.
Syrel, the medic. Shaedra, the blade leader. Both captains. Both dangerous.
The duel slowed. Not from exhaustion. From decision.
They stepped back. At the same time. No winner. No loss. Just silence.
Syrel's gaze flicked to me again. Longer this time. Lingering on my throat. On the marks. Then she turned. Left.
Shaedra watched her go. Then looked at me. A slow smile spread across her face.

She stepped past me. Close enough that her shoulder brushed mine. Intentional. Claiming. And I stood there. Between them. Breathing. Understanding something I didn't want to understand. This wasn't just training. It was territory. And somehow…I had become part of it.
Twice a week. That was the only time Hannahrial allowed me near her silks.
Not the blood-stiffened leathers I scrubbed daily. Not the rain-soaked cloaks, the armor, the straps that smelled of iron and long marches.
Her silks were different. They felt… human. Soft in a way that didn't belong in this place. And she trusted me with them. That was what made it dangerous.

The Rain Hall was already full. Steam poured out in thick, rolling waves, carrying laughter, water, the low murmur of voices that had never known restraint. I stepped inside anyway, head lowered, arms tight around the folded silks.
I made it three steps. Then…a sharp strike behind my knee. I dropped. Hard. The cloth slipped from my hands but I caught it before it touched the wet stone.
The twins. Always the twins. One of them nudged my shoulder with her foot. Not enough to hurt. Enough to remind.
Laughter followed me out. I didn't look back.

The cold hit harder outside. Not because the air had changed. Because I had. I moved fast. Past the main paths. Past the noise. Further west than I had any reason to go. I told myself I just needed water.

Somewhere quiet. Somewhere empty. The camp thinned. Then disappeared. The Grove didn't announce itself. It swallowed you. The trees thickened, roots breaking through the ground like old bones. The air grew heavy. Not cold. Not warm. Just… thick. Like something breathing too slowly beneath it.

And then..the lake. Black. Perfectly still. It didn't reflect the sky. Didn't reflect me. It looked like a hole carved into the world. Mist drifted across it in slow, deliberate movements, as if it had purpose. As if it knew something I didn't.
I shouldn't have stepped closer. I knew that. My body knew that. But I did.
The silks slipped slightly in my grip as I knelt. The ground was damp here. Soft. Too soft. I reached out. The water touched my fingers..and something inside me recoiled. Not pain. Recognition.
I dipped the silk. The surface swallowed it. No ripple. No resistance.
Syrel stood behind me. Close enough that I hadn't heard her approach. Close enough that I should have.
I didn't move. I couldn't. Her hand closed around my wrist. Not harsh. Firm. Warm.
I pulled the silk from the water. It looked unchanged. But it felt wrong. Heavy. As if it had absorbed something I couldn't see.
She took it from me. Dropped it onto the earth. Careless. Like it was already ruined.
Her voice was quieter now. Not anger. Something tighter.
She didn't answer immediately. Her gaze drifted past me. To the lake. For a moment…her face changed. Not cold. Not sharp. Remembering.
"This place was here before we were."
Her fingers loosened slightly around my wrist, but she didn't let go.
"Before the camp. Before the walls. Before the Queen ever named the Vale."
The mist shifted across the surface. Slow. Intentional.
"The first Rangers tried to claim it."
Her thumb brushed lightly against my pulse. Absentminded.
"The first time, the water vanished for a night."
Her grip tightened slightly. Not enough to hurt. Enough to hold.
Her eyes flicked to me. Watching. Measuring.
Her fingers shifted. Sliding up my wrist.
My stomach dropped. Her hand moved higher. To my forearm. Tracing. Light.
The lake didn't move. Didn't react. Didn't acknowledge.
I shouldn't have asked. Her hand slid to my throat. Right over the marks. Shaedra's marks.
Her thumb pressed lightly. Not pain. Not quite.
Silence. I didn't breathe. Her fingers traced the bruises there slowly. Carefully. Almost gently.
I swallowed. Hard. Her hand lingered. Longer than it should have.
The words were quiet. Not rejection. Warning. Then she released me.
I followed. Of course I did. Back through the Grove. But slower now. Closer. She didn't walk ahead of me this time. She walked beside me. Sometimes, her shoulder brushed mine. Not accidental.
Back into the camp. Into the quieter corridors. Into the medical wing. Her chambers were… different.
Not warm. Not soft. But ordered. Controlled. Safe. A basin stood against the wall. Clear water. Still. She placed the silks beside it.
I nodded. I didn't argue. My hands moved automatically. Water. Cloth. Careful. Gentle. But I felt her watching. Not like Shaedra. Not hungry. Focused. Studying.
Her fingers touched my throat again. Light. Tracing the marks. Something flickered across her face. Something I didn't understand.
It wasn't a question. I didn't answer. Her thumb pressed slightly harder.

The word came out softer than anything I had ever heard from her. I looked up. Her eyes met mine. And for a moment…they weren't cold. They were something worse. Something that made my chest tighten. Because it felt like. care.
She turned away. But didn't leave. And as I washed Hannah's silks in her chamber carefully, slowly, exactly as she had shown me.
The basin water stilled as I finished.
The last of the silk slipped between my fingers, light again, clean, almost untouched by the world it lived in. I folded it carefully, slower than necessary, more to delay than out of precision.
She hadn't left. I could feel her there. Behind me. Still watching. Not pressing. Not forcing. Just… there.
I turned. My hands felt heavier now that they were empty. I didn't think. For once, I didn't think. I reached out. And took her hand.
She stilled. Not violently. Not sharply. Just… still.
The words came out softer than I intended. Not forced. Not careful. Just honest. Her fingers didn't pull away. Not immediately.

Her gaze dropped to where our hands met. Then back to my face. Something in her expression shifted. Her free hand lifted. Slow. Careful. And touched my face. Not like before. Not clinical. Not measuring. Gentle. Her fingers rested against my cheek, cool against my skin, tracing lightly as if confirming something. As if remembering something.
I hesitated. For the first time in a long time. Not out of fear. Out of uncertainty.
Her brow tightened slightly. Not in anger. In warning.
I should have stopped. I didn't.
The moment the words left my mouth..her hand froze. Then, she recoiled. Not violently. But sharply enough that I felt it. Her expression twisted. Disgust. Immediate. Unfiltered.
Her hand dropped from my face like she had touched something wrong. Something she shouldn't have.
I stepped back. My chest tightening instantly.
The word came out too fast. Too sharp. Silence filled the room. Heavy. Unforgiving.
I lowered my gaze. Of course. Of course that was wrong. Everything I touched here turned wrong.
My voice felt smaller again. Like it had shrunk back into the shape this place expected. She didn't respond. Seconds passed. Too long. Then..her breathing shifted. Just slightly.
I did. Slowly. The disgust was gone. Not replaced. Changed. Her eyes searched my face. Not for defiance. Not for arrogance. For something else. And whatever she found, softened something in her.
Her voice was quieter now. Lower. I shook my head.

I stopped. Because I didn't know how to explain it. Not properly. She exhaled slowly. Her hand lifted again. This time slower. More careful. And rested against my shoulder. Not pushing. Not controlling. Holding.
Then, she pulled me forward. Into her. The embrace wasn't tight. Not crushing. But it was firm. Protective.
My body stiffened for a second, then gave. Because I hadn't realized how much I needed that. Her hand rested against the back of my head. Not forcing. Guiding.
My grip tightened slightly against her. Before I could stop myself.
The words landed differently. Heavier. My chest tightened again. But not from fear this time. Something else. Something warm. My heart… fluttered. I pulled back slightly. Reluctantly.
The question felt fragile the moment it left my mouth.
Syrel's expression shifted again. Not anger. Not fear. Calculation. She stepped back. Creating space.
The word wasn't harsh. But it was firm.
Of course. Nothing here was ever simple.
I nodded. Of course I did.
Hannah chamber felt larger than usual. Or maybe I felt smaller. I entered. Carefully. The folded silks held tightly in my arms.
She sat this time. Not standing. Not moving. Watching.
"Then why are you breathing like that?"
Her wardrobe was… immaculate. Ordered. Precise. Every piece folded, placed, aligned. I stepped inside.
Placed the silks where they belonged. Tried to match the spacing. The angles. The control.
Her voice came from behind me. I froze. She stepped closer. Into the space. Too close. Her hand adjusted the fold. Precise. Perfect.
The word stung more than it should have.
Her hand struck. Fast. Across my jaw. My head snapped to the side. Pain flared.
Her gaze cut into me. I hesitated. Just for a second. That was enough.
Her hand grabbed my collar. Pulled me closer.
I swallowed the rest of my words. But something slipped anyway.
"She said she would speak to you.."
The second strike came harder. My vision flashed white. I dropped to my knees.
"You do not use my captains to bargain with me."
Her voice wasn't raised. It didn't need to be.
Her hand gripped my chin. Forced my head up.
"You do not repeat what they offer."
"You do not bring their influence into my chamber."
"You meant to move above your place."
The words landed like weight. Final.
"You meant to use what is not yours."
Silence crushed the space around us.
The meaning settled slowly. Then all at once.
The word slipped out before I could stop it. Her hand moved. My breath caught as she struck again. Not as hard. But enough.
I went still. Because I understood. This wasn't punishment. Not just that. This was correction. Reclaiming. Control.
"You will not leave this chamber tonight."
I nodded. Slowly. Because I had no choice.
She released me. Turned away. Like the matter was settled. Because to her, it was.

I remained there. On my knees. My cheek burning. My chest tight. My thoughts scattered. Because just hours ago, I had felt something close to safety. Something close to warmth. And now, I was reminded exactly what this place was.
The silence stretched, thick and suffocating, broken only by the faint sound of fabric shifting as she moved about her chamber as if nothing had happened.
As if I wasn't still there. Waiting. Breathing too loudly. Thinking too much.
I didn't want to stay here. Not tonight. Not like this. Not after, Syrel's arms came back to me. The way she had held me. The way her voice had softened. If it gets too much… come back.
My chest tightened. I couldn't go back. I couldn't leave. I looked up. She hadn't dismissed me. She hadn't acknowledged me. I was just… there.
I need that warmth again..and I remembered the letter. Who Captain Hannah really is, to me. I had to try. At least once.
My voice failed. I swallowed. Tried again.
The word slipped out quietly. Fragile. Almost hopeful.
Everything stopped. Not loudly. Not sharply. But completely. Hannah turned. Slowly. Her gaze settled on me. There was no confusion in it. No hesitation. Only..cold recognition.
The command was quiet. Unavoidable. My chest rose and fell unevenly.
"…it might be easier… if I could think of you as.."
Her hand moved. I didn't even see it. Pain exploded across my face as the strike landed, harder than before.
I fell sideways, my shoulder hitting the floor, breath knocked from my lungs.
Her voice cut through the air like a blade. I tried to push myself up. Failed.
"You do not place yourself in my blood."
Her footsteps approached. Measured. Controlled. I felt her presence before I saw her again. Her hand caught my jaw. Forced my head up.
"You do not name me with titles you have not earned."
"You think because you were held by one of my captains, that.."
The words hit harder than the strike.
Her thumb pressed into my jaw. Pain flared.
"You are not here to feel comfortable."
Her face leaned closer. Not warm. Not kind.
"You are here to be made correct."
"I just didn't want to be alone…"
For a moment, something in her gaze shifted. Not softened. Measured. Then gone.
"And you will remain so until you understand why."

She released me. I collapsed back onto the floor. Breathing hard. My cheek throbbing. My chest tight. I stayed there. Because I had nowhere else to go. Because she wouldn't let me leave. Because I had tried to take something that didn't belong to me. Again. And now, I was paying for it.

The chamber felt colder than ever. Larger. Empty in a way that pressed in on me. Syrel's warmth felt distant now. Unreal. Like something imagined. And Hannah stood just a few steps away. Close enough to touch. But further than anything I had ever known.

I curled slightly where I lay. Not by choice. My body simply gave. And for the first time that night, I understood something clearly. Warmth here, was not something you could ask for. Only something you survived long enough…to maybe be allowed near. And even then, it would cost you.
I did not leave. I couldn't.

Her command still hung in the air like something physical, pressing against my chest, settling into my bones. The door behind me remained open for a moment longer… then closed with a quiet finality that made something in me tighten.
It wasn't a suggestion. It wasn't a kindness. It was a boundary drawn around me.

I stood there, unsure where to put my hands, where to look, how to breathe without doing it wrong. Her chamber felt different at night. Larger. Quieter. The flickering candlelight softened the hard edges of everything, but it didn't make it warmer. Nothing in this place was warm.
She moved without looking at me.

The sound of silk brushing against itself was soft, deliberate. Red against shadow. I tried not to stare, but my eyes kept drifting back to her. Not because of the way she looked, but because of how she occupied the space. Even without armor, without command, without the camp around her..she still felt like something I wasn't allowed to reach.
My body reacted before my mind did. I stepped forward, each movement measured, careful, as if the floor itself might betray me if I moved too quickly.
Her hand lifted slightly, barely a gesture, but enough.
I stepped again, until I could feel the subtle shift in the air around her. Not warmth. Never warmth. Just… presence. I lowered my gaze.

And immediately regretted it. Not because of anger. Not because of punishment. Because she was watching me too closely. Not like a commander. Like she was trying to understand something she didn't quite trust.
My throat tightened. "I don't want to make mistakes."
Her voice was quiet, but it landed heavier than anything shouted.
"I thought that was what I was supposed to do."
Her eyes narrowed slightly. Not in anger. In correction.
"You think because I have allowed you to remain… that you are meant to understand."
I didn't answer. I didn't know how to.
She stepped closer. One step. That was all it took. Her hand rose, not quickly, not harshly, and then her fingers were at my jaw, lifting it just slightly so I couldn't look away.
"You are not here to understand yet."
Her thumb pressed lightly against my cheek, just enough to remind me of the earlier strike. It still burned. Still lingered.
"You are here to learn your place."
Her hand lingered a second longer than necessary. Then released.
I froze. Just for a second. That was enough. Her eyes sharpened.
I bent quickly, fingers fumbling slightly as I pulled them off, setting them aside carefully, as if even that could be judged.
She turned away from me then, moving toward the bed. It was too large for one person. Too deliberate. Everything about it felt like a statement I didn't understand yet.
The clarification came without her turning.
"You will not move closer than I allow."
"You will not mistake this for comfort."
She finally looked at me again.
And for a moment..something shifted. Not softer. Not kinder. But… quieter.
The words weren't harsh. They were worse. They were tired.

I stepped forward and moved to the edge of the bed, sitting carefully, unsure how much space I was allowed to take. The fabric beneath me was softer than anything I had felt in weeks. It made my body feel heavier. Like I didn't belong on it.
She moved around the other side. Slowly. Deliberately. Then sat. Not close. Not far. Just enough distance that I was aware of her. Constantly.
I obeyed. Carefully. Rigidly. Every part of me tense, waiting for correction. The silence stretched. Long. Uncomfortable. My eyes stayed open. I didn't dare close them.
I hadn't realized I wasn't. I forced myself to inhale slowly. Then again. Then again.
Her gaze shifted slightly, studying me again.
My chest tightened. The words came before I could stop them.
Silence. Heavy. Dangerous. I expected a strike. A correction. A dismissal. Instead, she leaned back slightly, her gaze drifting toward the ceiling.
The name hit me immediately. My chest tightened again.
Her voice had changed. Not softer. Just… less sharp.
I turned my head slightly, just enough to see her.
"You do not become her by feeling the same things."
Her eyes shifted toward me again.
"You become her if you act on them without thinking."
Silence settled again. But it felt different now. Not empty. Just… controlled.
I stared at the ceiling, trying to slow my breathing, trying to understand what I was supposed to do with any of this.

The word slipped out before I could stop it. Everything in the room stopped. Not loudly. Not suddenly. Just… completely. My chest dropped. I turned my head slightly toward her. She hadn't moved. Not yet.
Her voice was calm. That made it worse.
The strike came instantly. Sharp. Clean.
My head snapped to the side, the sting exploding across my cheek as I sucked in a breath I couldn't control. I pushed myself up slightly.
Her hand was already there, gripping my jaw, forcing me back down.
"You do not name me like that."
Her voice was low now. Dangerous.
"You do not take titles that are not given."
"You are not in a position to think what I am to you."
"You were trying to make this easier."
